To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) refugees experience high rates of mental health problems, and (2) the mental health of refugees is influenced by multiple factors.
the mental health of refugees and asylum seekers is influenced by the direct effects of war exposure as well as by the indirect effects of ongoing displacement-related stressors.

the mental health of displaced populations can be conceptualized using an ecological model of distress that considers the direct effects of war exposure, as well as the effects of ongoing displacement-related stressors that include social, economic, and legal stressors, and stressors associated with the process of resettlement in a host country.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of an ecological model of the mental health of refugees and other civilians displaced by armed conflicts.
understanding and alleviating the suffering of people who have been forcibly displaced by armed conflict and other human-caused disasters.
the effects of displacement on the mental health and wellbeing of refugees and other forcibly displaced people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is a strong association between the mental health of refugees and their pre-migration exposure to trauma, and that the mental health of these populations may be improved by addressing the ongoing stressors associated with their displacement.

the mental health and psychological needs of refugees and displaced persons are best understood within an ecological perspective, which recognizes the multiple and complex stressors that are associated with the experience of displacement and the ongoing social, economic, and political conditions in the receiving countries.

the refugee experience is associated with a wide range of psychological difficulties, and that the mental health needs of refugees should be addressed through the development and implementation of culturally sensitive, comprehensive, and integrated mental health services.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mental health of displaced civilians is shaped by a dynamic interplay between war exposure and displacement-related stressors, and that interventions must address the needs of displaced populations across the full spectrum of the refugee experience, from preflight trauma to post-migration adjustment.

there is an association between the mental health status of the host community, the mental health status and needs of the refugees, and the quality of the relationship between the host community and the refugees.

we found that the most important factors for predicting the mental health of refugees and asylum seekers were not the factors related to the war exposure, but rather the factors related to their displacement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mental health interventions should focus not only on the direct effects on trauma, but also the ongoing stressors of displacement.

mental health among displaced persons stems not only from the prior war exposure, which is often the focus of humanitarian efforts, but also from ongoing stressors in a refugee’s social ecology, or what we call displacement-related stressors.
mental health among civilians displaced by armed violence is shaped by a complex array of risk and protective factors that are not well captured in the traditional war exposure model.
